summary: I verified every claimed fix against the staged bytes rather than against the account of them, and all five are really there this time. R2b: the sentence 'a different incarnationId is a new incarnation and is accepted' is gone -- ADR-0036:57 now reads only 'A different incarnationId is accepted, which is the case the bare pair got wrong', and :72-81 adds the UNORDERED-is-a-price paragraph with the X/Y slot-overwrite worked example (X commits (Ix,5), Y commits (Iy,3) and takes the slot, X's retry of 5 is tested against a foreign watermark and accepted) and the explicit 'ADR-0031 DOES NOT COVER IT'. R3a: 'Which formats change' :92-96 now carries the four-field slot podId -> (incarnationId, lastAppliedFlushSeq, epoch, sequence) and says the pointer is normative there rather than only in Consequences; the ADR-0033 banner (0033-...md:6-10) and M4.10c's row (backlog.md:123) carry the same shape. R3b: :60-70 adds the answer-or-refuse rule. R3c: backlog-done.md:149 now says 'minted per INGESTER process', matching the ADR's own load-bearing minting clause. Minors: :138-140 says about 32 bytes per pod in both the field list and the conclusion, and the 175/200 is caveated as a fixture artifact at :27-30 as well as in the M4.46 notes. The decision itself is now stronger than at round 3: the key discriminates a restart, the checkpoint stays one entry per pod, detection is an in-memory comparison and no steady-state commit-path request scales with pods, shards or indices, and the pre-upgrade-checkpoint hazard is answered in the direction that accepts rather than suppresses. What does not hold together is the R3b fix itself, and its reach. The refusal branch's safety argument is false in the only case that reaches it, and the remedy it prescribes commits already-committed records a second time -- and the answer-or-refuse rule is stated in one of the three places in this commit that prescribe the behaviour, the other two (the ADR's own Consequences, and M4.10d's row rewritten by this same commit) still saying answer unconditionally with the original offsets. That is round 3's finding fixed in the Decision section and left standing in the section and the row an implementer builds from, which is the shape of R3a with the sections swapped.

findings.summary: THE REFUSAL BRANCH'S SAFETY ARGUMENT IS FALSE, AND THE REMEDY IT PRESCRIBES DUPLICATES. The new paragraph ends: 'Refusing neither duplicates nor suppresses: nothing applied under that key, and the caller can re-flush.' The refusal fires only after detection has fired, and detection is 'flushSeq <= lastAppliedFlushSeq for the same (podId, incarnationId)' over a flushSeq the same ADR calls 'dense and monotone within an incarnation' (:52-54). Every flushSeq at or below the watermark for that incarnation therefore DID apply. So 'nothing applied under that key' is false in every case that reaches the refusal -- it is not a case where the commit is unknown, it is the case where the commit is known to have landed and the offsets are merely unreachable. And 're-flush' is defined by this ADR's own Consequences (:163-167): 'a producer-level retry is a NEW flush under a new key with an incremented flushSeq -- not a replay at all'. Verified in the tree: DefaultIngest.flushLocked publishes a fresh segment and calls sequencer.commit(new CommitRequest(podShortId, flushSeq++, ...)) (DefaultIngest.java:344-348), and on failure completes every waiter exceptionally and rethrows (:385-390), so nothing resubmits the same key.
findings.failure_scenario: Pod poda, incarnation I. Flush 4 commits in delta (e,10); flush 5 commits in delta (e,11); the slot holds lastApplied=5 and the pointer to (e,11). A duplicate of flushSeq 4 arrives -- the case this paragraph was written for, and the case the Decision names at :55-57 as reachable through commitAll. Detection fires. The pointed delta does not carry (poda,I,4), so M4.10d refuses with the prescribed distinguishable error. The ingester then follows the ADR: it re-flushes. The same records are published under a new segment key and committed under (poda,I,6), and the log now carries those records TWICE, at two disjoint offset ranges, with two acknowledgements. That is duplication of committed records -- the thing FR-3 and this ADR exist to prevent -- produced by following the ADR's own sentence, and it is worse than the wrong-offset answer the paragraph rejects, because a consumer sees the records twice rather than one caller seeing a wrong offset. The alternative reading, that the caller should instead drop the flush, is the opposite instruction and is nowhere in the ADR. ⚠️ Reachability is not a corner: after M7's retention starts pruning deltas the pointer will also dangle (ADR-0033:33 -- the chain grows 'until M7's retention deletes anything'), and a failed GET lands in the same refusal branch.
findings.suggestion: Decide what a refusal MEANS and say it, because M4.10d implements this sentence. If refusing is right, the error says 'this (podId, incarnationId, flushSeq) is already committed; its offsets are not recoverable' and the ADR states plainly that the caller must NOT re-flush -- and then owes one sentence on what the ingester does with a flush it can neither ack nor retry. If re-flushing is meant to be safe, the design has to make the refusal unreachable (e.g. answer from the recovered tail state the CommitDelta triple already rebuilds, which covers every flushSeq above the newest checkpoint, and refuse only below it), and the ADR should say so. Either way delete 'nothing applied under that key': in the branch that reaches it, something always did.

findings.summary: THE ANSWER-OR-REFUSE RULE LANDED IN ONE OF THE THREE PLACES THIS COMMIT PRESCRIBES THE BEHAVIOUR. Decision :60-70 now says a replay is answered from the pointed delta ONLY if it carries the exact triple, and refused otherwise. Consequences, unchanged this round, still ends 'The delta it points at carries SegmentCommit.segmentKey and RunCommit.firstOffset, an absolute offset (ADR-0001), so one GET answers the replay' (:124-125) -- the unqualified sentence round 3 named, with no refusal branch and no bound. And M4.10d's row, REWRITTEN BY THIS COMMIT, says 'a replay is flushSeq <= lastApplied for the same incarnation, answered with the ORIGINAL offsets' (backlog.md:124), with the refusal branch absent there and absent from its notes section, which this commit also rewrote. M4.10c's row and the ADR-0033 banner were both propagated to the new slot shape; the row that will implement the answering rule was not.
findings.failure_scenario: A session picks M4.10d. Its row is the task. The row says a detected replay is answered with the original offsets, unconditionally; the notes it is told to read say only 'Refuse a replayed (podId, incarnationId, flushSeq)' plus an update-rule warning; if it opens the ADR at all, the Consequences paragraph that justifies the pointer tells it one GET answers the replay. Two of three durable statements say answer, one says answer-or-refuse. It implements the majority: GET the pointed delta, return its firstOffset. For any replay below the watermark it hands back another flush's offsets -- exactly the M4.46-class violation the Decision section added this round to forbid ('a committed offset resolves to the records committed at it'), shipped with a green suite, because a test written from the row asserts the original offsets come back and a single-flush fixture makes the pointed delta the right one.
findings.suggestion: Put the bound in M4.10d's row and its notes in the same words as the Decision -- answered from the pointed delta only when it carries the exact triple, refused with a distinguishable error otherwise -- and qualify the Consequences sentence so it stops claiming one GET answers every replay. This is the same propagation the commit already did for M4.10c; it is one row short.

findings.summary: THE ADR SAYS ITS OWN AMENDMENT IS SMALLER THAN THE AMENDMENT IT WROTE. ADR-0033's banner, added by this commit, says the per-pod lastAppliedFlushSeq 'gains an incarnationId and a pointer to the delta that last applied'. ADR-0036's Consequences restatement of the same amendment, three sections later, still says only 'its per-pod lastAppliedFlushSeq gains an incarnationId beside it' -- no pointer, which is the field round 3's finding was about.
findings.failure_scenario: A reader reconciling the two ADRs finds the amending document describing a two-field slot and the amended document describing a three-part one. Nothing is mis-encoded, because 'Which formats change' is normative and correct, so this is minor -- but it is the last copy of the pre-pointer shape in the tree, and the next session to grep for what ADR-0033 became can land on it.
findings.suggestion: Add 'and a pointer to the delta that last applied' to the Consequences sentence, matching the banner.

findings.summary: 'NO COMMIT-PATH REQUEST SCALES WITH PODS' IS ARGUED FOR DETECTION ONLY, AND THE ADR ADDS A CONDITIONAL COMMIT-PATH GET. The heading is unqualified; the sentence under it covers detection ('an in-memory comparison against state recovered once per takeover') and is silent on answering, which this same ADR says costs one GET of the pointed delta (:124-125). The task's own property list singles this axis out -- 'no COMMIT-PATH request that scales with the number of pods -- the rate M4.7 was built to remove' -- so the claim is the one a later session will quote.
findings.failure_scenario: A sequencer failover leaves one in-flight commit per pod ambiguous, and every pod retries once the new leader is up. Each retry that is a replay costs one GET before it can be answered, so the failover burst issues one extra GET per pod on the commit path. That is a per-node rate and permitted, and it is bounded by one GET per replayed commit rather than per pod per commit, so it is not the M4.7 rate returning -- but the ADR's paragraph asserts the stronger property it did not check, and a future change that makes answering cost two GETs, or that walks, will be measured against a sentence that already said zero.
findings.suggestion: One clause: detection adds no request; answering costs one GET per DETECTED REPLAY, which scales with retries and pods-in-a-retry-storm, not with commits, records, shards or indices.
